questions.prompt: You open your eyes in the morning. What do you do first?

options.label: Open the curtains or drink some water

insight.reveal: Your response indicates an instinct to look after the basics before anything else claims your attention. People with this orientation tend to tidy the room before tackling the problem, keep a water bottle within reach at work, and are often the steady friend who notices when everyone else has forgotten to eat.
insight.step: Tomorrow morning, notice the very first thought you have before you move. Just notice it.

options.label: Reach for my phone

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests your day often opens with other people's news before your own thoughts get a word in. You are likely to be quick to respond and well informed, the one who knows what happened overnight, while your best ideas tend to arrive later, in the shower or on a walk, once the screen is out of reach.
insight.step: Tomorrow, wait until your feet touch the floor before you touch your phone.

options.label: Snooze, then snooze again

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a soft spot for comfort now, even if it means a rushed start later. People who snooze tend to make the same small trade elsewhere, like replying 'later' to messages they actually want to answer, yet they are often surprisingly good under time pressure, out of the door in record time.
insight.step: Next time your alarm rings, sit up before you decide anything. See if the bargain feels different sitting up.

options.label: Lie still and replay yesterday or worry about today

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a mind that tends to wake up before your body does. People like this often replay small social moments rather than big problems, wondering how a comment landed, and the thoughts usually settle once their hands are busy. That same attentiveness tends to make them unusually thoughtful about how others feel.
insight.step: Tomorrow, when the replay starts, get up and do one physical thing, like making the bed, before you keep thinking.

followUp.prompt: How did the first few minutes after waking set the tone for your day?

options.label: I started slowly and felt steady
options.reflection: A gentle start often carries further than it seems. When your first minutes belong to you, the rest of the day tends to follow that pace. Tomorrow, see if you can keep just one of those quiet minutes for yourself again.

options.label: My phone had me before I was really up
options.reflection: Days that open on a screen can feel a little borrowed, as if they began without you. That's very common, not a failing. Tomorrow, you might give yourself one small thing first, a stretch or a glass of water, before the world comes in.

options.label: Worries arrived before I'd even got up
options.reflection: When worries get in early, the whole day can feel like it's playing catch-up with your mind. That tends to ease once your body moves first. Tomorrow, you could try sitting up and putting your feet on the floor before you let a thought finish.

options.label: Honestly, it was a blur
options.reflection: Some mornings pass without leaving much of a mark, and that's okay. Your attention may simply have been needed elsewhere. Tomorrow, you could pause for one slow breath when you first sit up and notice how the day feels from there.

questions.prompt: You miss one day of a habit you were building. What happens next?

options.label: I just pick it up again the next day

insight.reveal: Your response indicates you judge a habit by the month, not by the day. People with this outlook tend to bounce back from slips without drama, and the same wide view often shows up in friendships: one missed call or a forgotten birthday rarely changes how you see someone you care about.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: This week, give one habit a 'never miss twice' rule and see how it feels.

options.label: I do double the next day to make up for it

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you keep a quiet ledger with yourself. People who 'pay back' missed days are often the same ones who return favours quickly, repay small loans before being asked and feel uneasy owing anyone anything. That makes you deeply dependable, even if you can be a tough creditor to yourself.
insight.step: Next time you miss a day, do the normal amount, not double. Notice if the ledger voice complains.

options.label: I quietly let the whole habit go

insight.reveal: Your answer points to an all-or-nothing view of habits: once the chain breaks, it can feel finished. The same feeling tends to show up with diets, learning and tidying. The upside is that you often throw yourself into fresh starts with real energy, and a gentler restart rule can help that energy last.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: Pick one habit you dropped and do the smallest version of it once this week, just one minute.

options.label: I feel it proves something about me

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a tendency to turn one missed day into a verdict on your whole character. People like this are often very fair judges of other people's slips and very strict judges of their own. That same high standard is usually why friends and colleagues trust you to take things seriously.
insight.step: Next time you slip, ask: 'What would I say to a friend who missed one day?' Then say that to yourself.

followUp.prompt: How did a habit you're building go today?

options.label: I kept it up, even if only a small version
options.reflection: Keeping a habit going on an ordinary day, even in a smaller form, is often what makes it stick. You may be learning that showing up matters more than doing it perfectly. Tomorrow, let a small version count again if that's all there's room for.

options.label: I skipped it and I'm okay with that
options.reflection: Missing a day without turning it into a verdict on yourself is a quiet strength. Habits tend to survive gaps when there's no shame attached. Tomorrow, you could simply pick it back up as if today were just a pause.

options.label: I skipped it and I'm being hard on myself
options.reflection: It sounds like a missed day may have felt bigger than it was. One skip rarely undoes a habit, though a harsh inner voice can make it feel that way. Tomorrow, you might try the smallest possible version and let that be enough.

options.label: I'm not building a habit right now
options.reflection: Not every season is for building new habits, and there's nothing wrong with that. Sometimes keeping your days steady is the work. If something small calls to you tomorrow, you could simply notice it without needing to start.

questions.prompt: Your desk or table right now looks like…

options.label: Clear, with everything in its place

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a mind that thinks more freely once things are put away, as if the table were part of your head. People like this tend to tidy right before a hard task, not to avoid it but to warm up, and are often the one at work who can find any document within seconds.
insight.step: Before your next hard task, give yourself exactly two minutes to tidy, then start, even if it's not done.

options.label: Piles that only I understand

insight.reveal: Picking this suggests you remember things by where they are rather than by labels. People with this style often thrive with loose, flexible systems, can pull the right paper from a stack instantly, and feel oddly lost when someone 'helpfully' tidies their space for them.
insight.step: This week, notice how fast you can find one thing in your piles. Your system may be better than it looks.

options.label: Buried, and I'll fix it on some big day

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a quiet belief in a future 'big day' when everything gets sorted at once. People who wait for that day often wait for it elsewhere too, with inbox clean-ups or calling old friends. The strength hiding here: when the big day does come, you tend to tackle it with impressive bursts of energy.
insight.step: Today, clear just one corner of the table, the size of a book. Stop there.

options.label: Honestly, it looks like how my head feels

insight.reveal: This answer reflects an honest awareness that your space and your mood tend to move together. People like this are often finely tuned to atmosphere, and the link runs both ways: clearing one small corner of the table can sometimes lift a cloudy day more than you would expect.
insight.step: On your next heavy day, clear one small surface and check if your mood shifts, even slightly.

followUp.prompt: How did your desk or table look by the end of today?

options.label: I cleared it before I finished
options.reflection: Clearing your space at the end of the day can be a way of closing the door on work. It often makes the next morning feel lighter. Tomorrow, you might notice whether starting at a clear surface changes how quickly you settle in.

options.label: Messier, but I know where everything is
options.reflection: A busy surface can be a sign of a busy, working mind, and you may have your own quiet system in the piles. If it serves you, it serves you. Tomorrow, you might just check whether the mess is helping you or slowing you down.

options.label: It got worse and it's bothering me
options.reflection: When a cluttered space starts to bother you, it can be a sign that your head feels full too. You don't need to fix it all at once. Tomorrow, you could clear just one small corner and see if your thoughts feel a little roomier.

options.label: I wasn't at a desk or table much today
options.reflection: Some days happen away from any desk, on your feet or on the move. That can be a welcome change. Tomorrow, if you do sit down somewhere, you might notice what the space around you says about your mood.

questions.prompt: When do you usually start a new habit?

options.label: On a Monday or the first of the month

insight.reveal: Your response indicates you like a clean line between the old you and the new one. People with this orientation tend to love new calendars, fresh notebooks and Monday plans, and often bring real commitment to a new start. The hidden cost: if the line is missed, the next start can feel a whole week or month away.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Pick one small habit and start it on an ordinary day this week, like a Thursday.

options.label: Right now, the moment the idea hits

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests energy is your fuel more than planning. People like this tend to start many things with real joy and pull others in with their enthusiasm, and the habits that last are usually the ones tied to something they already do every day, like the morning coffee or the commute.
insight.step: Attach one new habit to something you already do daily: 'After I make tea, I will…'

options.label: After I find the best way to do it

insight.reveal: Your answer points to wanting to start right more than start soon. People like this tend to read every review before buying, compare options across many open tabs, and then pause for a long while before choosing. The upside is that when you do commit, you rarely have to undo the decision.
insight.step: This week, start one habit with the 'good enough' method, then improve it after three days.

options.label: I keep planning it but rarely begin

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how much you enjoy the planned version of yourself. Planning feels like progress, so the mind gets a small reward without the hard part. People like this are often excellent at seeing the big picture, and the missing piece tends to be a clear trigger rather than motivation.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Write a when-then plan for one habit: 'When I sit down after dinner, I will…'

followUp.prompt: Did you start, or think about starting, something new today?

options.label: I just began, right then and there
options.reflection: Starting the moment an idea lands takes a kind of trust in yourself. It often means you learn by doing rather than by planning. Tomorrow, you might give the new thing ten minutes again and see if it still feels alive.

options.label: I picked a fresh day to start
options.reflection: Choosing a clean start date can help you feel ready and give the new thing a proper welcome. The tricky part tends to be keeping that date. Tomorrow, you could write it down somewhere you'll see it, so your future self remembers.

options.label: I thought about it again but didn't begin
options.reflection: Coming back to the same idea again and again can mean it really matters to you, even if it hasn't started yet. Sometimes the first step just needs to be smaller. Tomorrow, you could try a tiny version of it, with no promise to continue.

options.label: Nothing new was on my mind today
options.reflection: Days without a new project can be restful, a chance to live with what you already have. You don't always need something to work on. Tomorrow, you might notice if any small curiosity tugs at you, and just let it be there.

questions.prompt: You're stuck waiting in a line for ten minutes. What do you do?

options.label: Watch the people around me

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a natural curiosity about the people around you. Those who watch others in a queue tend to collect small stories without noticing, read a room quickly at parties or meetings, and are often the first to sense when a friend's mood is off before anything is said.
insight.step: Next time you wait, guess one stranger's day from small clues. Just for fun.

options.label: Scroll on my phone

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you like every gap in the day to be filled with something. People like this tend to stay well informed and are rarely bored, yet they often say their mind feels oddly 'full' at night, because the empty minutes were where the mind used to tidy itself.
insight.step: In your next line, leave the phone in your pocket for the first two minutes.

options.label: Make plans or lists in my head

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a feeling that idle time is time you could be using. People like this are often the ones who remember birthdays and deadlines, carry a mental plan for the week, and find it surprisingly hard to switch off on holiday, even on a beach.
insight.step: Next time you wait, try to notice five sounds instead of making a plan.

options.label: Get restless and annoyed the whole time

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a full life more than a short temper. People who feel this in a queue are often juggling packed days, and the irritation is usually less about the line and more about losing control of their time. That same drive tends to make you efficient, the one who gets things moving at work.
insight.step: Next time you're stuck, decide on purpose what the ten minutes are for. See if choosing it changes the feeling.

followUp.prompt: Did you have to wait somewhere today? How did you spend the time?

options.label: I watched the people and things around me
options.reflection: Using a wait to look around suggests a mind that finds the world quietly interesting. Those small observations often stay with you. Tomorrow, you might notice one detail in a familiar place that you've never spotted before.

options.label: I went straight to my phone
options.reflection: Reaching for your phone in a wait is so common it barely feels like a choice. It can fill the time, though it rarely refreshes you. Next time you're waiting, you could try one minute of just looking around before you reach for it.

options.label: I got restless and a bit cross
options.reflection: Waiting can feel like time being taken from you, especially on a full day. Restlessness often means you had somewhere you'd rather be. Tomorrow, if you're stuck waiting, you could try a few slow breaths and see if the minutes soften.

options.label: There was no real waiting today
options.reflection: A day without queues or delays can feel smooth, or simply very full. Either way, you kept moving. Tomorrow, if a pause does come your way, you might treat it as a small gift of time rather than a delay.

questions.prompt: How do you keep track of things you need to do?

options.label: A written or phone list I really use

insight.reveal: Your response indicates you trust a system to hold what your mind would otherwise keep repeating. People with this habit tend to have quieter heads, sleep a little easier on busy weeks, and are often the person colleagues turn to when they need to know what was agreed.
insight.step: Tonight, add one thing that's been on your mind to your list and see if it stops repeating.

options.label: I keep it all in my head

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you trust your memory and enjoy freedom from systems. People like this tend to adapt quickly when plans change and hold on to the big things well, though the tiny ones have a habit of surfacing at two in the morning or just as you walk past the shop.
insight.step: For three days, write down only the tiny tasks. Keep the big ones in your head as usual.

options.label: I write lists, then lose them

insight.reveal: Your answer points to someone who gets the benefit from writing a list rather than reading it. Putting things on paper tends to calm your mind, so the list has often done its job before it goes missing. People like this are often good at sorting priorities in the moment, even without the note.
insight.step: Write tomorrow's list somewhere you'll see it by accident, like your phone's lock screen.

options.label: I add things I already did, just to tick them

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a wish for proof of a day well spent. Ticking off things you already did is a quiet way of telling yourself 'I was enough today', and many people secretly do it. Those who do tend to be hard workers who underestimate how much they actually get through.
insight.step: Tonight, write three things you did today that were never on any list.

followUp.prompt: How did you keep track of what needed doing today?

options.label: My list helped, and I ticked things off
options.reflection: A list you actually use can take a real weight off your mind. Ticking things off often gives a small, steady sense of progress. Tomorrow, you could try adding one thing that's just for you, not only for others.

options.label: I kept it all in my head and it worked
options.reflection: Holding the day in your head can work well when things are clear and familiar. It may also mean your mind stays a little on duty. Tomorrow, you could jot down just the one thing you'd hate to forget and see if it frees up some space.

options.label: Something slipped through the cracks
options.reflection: Letting something slip is part of having a full life, not a sign you're failing. It often happens when there's simply too much to hold. Tomorrow, you might write the most important thing somewhere you'll see it early on.

options.label: It was a light day, not much to track
options.reflection: A light day can be a welcome breather, a reminder that not every day has to be busy. Your mind may have had more room to wander. Tomorrow, you could notice whether that sense of space follows you into a fuller day.

questions.prompt: A free Saturday with no plans. By noon you've usually…

options.label: Done chores and errands

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that fun feels more allowed once the 'should' things are out of the way. People like this tend to clear the boring tasks first at work too, even when the exciting one matters more, and are often the friend whose fridge is stocked and whose bills are paid on time.
insight.step: Next free day, do one fun thing before any chore. Notice whether the fun feels earned or stolen.

options.label: Gone somewhere new

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests empty time feels to you like an invitation to explore. People like this tend to remember their year by places rather than dates, suggest the new restaurant instead of the usual one, and find that a week with no new sights feels oddly long.
insight.step: This week, take a different route to somewhere you go often.

options.label: Done nothing, and loved it

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a rare skill: resting without needing to justify it. People who can truly enjoy doing nothing tend to recover faster from busy weeks and stay calmer under pressure, though they often find guilt-free rest hard to explain to friends who fill every weekend.
insight.step: Protect one hour this weekend with nothing in it. Tell someone it's a plan.

options.label: Done nothing, and felt guilty about it

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a mind that tends to measure days by output. The surprise is that the guilt often takes more energy than the rest gives back, so a lazy day can leave you tired. The same drive is usually why people rely on you, and why you deserve rest that does not need earning.
insight.step: Next time you rest, give it a name in advance, like 'recharging time', and see if the guilt shrinks.

followUp.prompt: Did you get any free time today? How did you spend it?

options.label: I got chores and errands out of the way
options.reflection: Using free time to clear the decks can bring real relief and a tidy sense of control. Just watch that rest doesn't always come last. Tomorrow, you might let one free moment be for nothing useful at all.

options.label: I rested and really enjoyed it
options.reflection: Resting without needing to earn it is a lovely thing to be able to do. It often leaves you more ready for what comes next. Tomorrow, you could notice what made today's rest feel good, so you can find your way back to it.

options.label: I rested but felt I should be doing more
options.reflection: It sounds like rest came with a quiet voice saying you should be busy. Many people carry that voice, and it tends to steal the good part of resting. Tomorrow, you could try telling yourself that rest counts as something you did.

options.label: I had no free time today
options.reflection: A day with no free time can leave you running on empty by evening. That's worth noticing without blame. Tomorrow, you might look for even a few minutes that belong only to you, and protect them gently.

questions.prompt: At a café or restaurant you love, you usually order…

options.label: The same thing every time

insight.reveal: Your response indicates you like to save decision energy for the things that matter more. People who order the same favourite tend to know exactly what they like, stay loyal to places and brands, and often keep a small circle of very old friends they have known for years.
insight.step: Next visit, try one new item, but keep your favourite on the side as a safety net.

options.label: Something new each time

insight.reveal: Going with this suggests a small risk is part of the fun for you. People like this tend to enjoy planning trips, try the dish nobody can pronounce, and get restless when the weeks start looking the same. Friends often rely on you for recommendations.
insight.step: This week, bring the 'something new' rule to a different place, like the route home or a song.

options.label: Whatever the person with me gets

insight.reveal: Your answer points to someone who likes to keep things smooth and shared. People like this tend to be easy, warm company who put others at ease, though they sometimes lose track of what they themselves wanted, in bigger choices too, like holidays or where to live.
insight.step: Next time you eat out, decide your order before anyone else speaks.

options.label: I change my mind at the very last second

insight.reveal: This answer suggests your gut picks first and your doubt argues back. People who switch at the last second are often open to possibilities and quick to adapt, yet the first choice is frequently the one they truly wanted, and the switch is more about dodging regret than finding something better.
insight.step: Next time you order, keep your first choice and see if you enjoy it more.

followUp.prompt: When you picked something to eat or drink today, did you go for the usual or something new?

options.label: My usual, and it hit the spot
options.reflection: Going for the usual can be a small comfort, a way of knowing exactly what you'll get. On busy days, that's often a kindness to yourself. Tomorrow, you might notice whether it still feels like a choice or has quietly become a habit.

options.label: Something I'd never tried before
options.reflection: Trying something new, even something small, tends to keep life feeling fresh. It suggests you're open to a bit of surprise. Tomorrow, you could see where else a small new choice might fit, like a different route home.

options.label: Whatever the people with me were having
options.reflection: Going along with others can make shared moments easy and warm. It may also mean your own preferences take a back seat more than you notice. Tomorrow, you might try saying what you'd actually like, even in a small choice.

options.label: I didn't really think about it
options.reflection: Some days, food is just fuel and choices happen on autopilot. That's perfectly normal when your mind is busy elsewhere. Tomorrow, you could slow down for one meal or drink and really notice how it tastes.

questions.prompt: How many books, shows or projects do you have half-finished?

options.label: None, I finish what I start

insight.reveal: Your response indicates you feel a strong pull to close open loops. People like this tend to be reliable finishers at work and the friend who returns borrowed books. The twist: some also keep going with a series or a novel they stopped enjoying long ago, because stopping feels a little like losing.
insight.step: Choose one thing you're finishing out of duty, and give yourself permission to stop.

options.label: A couple, that's normal

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests a comfortable balance between curiosity and follow-through. People like you tend to finish what they love and let the rest go without much drama, which often makes you relaxed company and good at judging where your time is best spent.
insight.step: This week, finish one small thing you're close to the end of.

options.label: Lots, I love starting things

insight.reveal: Your answer points to someone who gets their joy from beginnings, when everything is new. People like this tend to have a lively mix of hobbies on the go, and the same pattern often shows up in friendships: easy, warm starts and lots of people they would love to see again.
insight.step: Pick one half-finished thing and do just one more step of it this week.

options.label: Lots, and they quietly weigh on me

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a habit of carrying your unfinished things like small stones in a bag. People like this tend to care deeply about their commitments, which is a real strength, and often find that officially deciding to stop something lifts the weight as much as finishing it would.
insight.step: Choose one unfinished thing and officially end it today. Say 'done' out loud.

followUp.prompt: Did any of your half-finished books, shows or projects come up today?

options.label: I finished one off
options.reflection: Finishing something can bring a clean, satisfying kind of relief. It often frees up energy you didn't know was tied up. Tomorrow, you might take a moment to enjoy that it's done before reaching for the next thing.

options.label: I started something new instead
options.reflection: The pull of something new can be hard to resist, and it often brings real joy. Starting is a gift in its own right. Tomorrow, you could choose one older thing and decide, kindly, whether to finish it or let it go.

options.label: I thought about them and felt the weight
options.reflection: Unfinished things can sit quietly on your shoulders, even when you're not working on them. You're allowed to put some down for good. Tomorrow, you might pick one and either take a small step or give yourself permission to leave it.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Some days the unfinished pile stays in the background, and that's fine. Not everything needs your attention at once. Tomorrow, if one of them crosses your mind, you might just notice how it makes you feel.

questions.prompt: You promised yourself one small thing today. By evening…

options.label: It's done

insight.reveal: Your response indicates you keep small promises to yourself, and that tends to build a quiet self-trust. People like this often find hard decisions less scary, come across as steady at work, and are likely to follow through on the plans they mention over dinner.
insight.step: Tomorrow, make yourself one tiny promise and keep it on purpose.

options.label: It's moved to tomorrow

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests 'tomorrow' is a place where many of your good intentions wait. People like this tend to be realistic about today's energy and kind to themselves on hard days, but tomorrow's self often ends up carrying the heaviest bag, and pinning the task to a specific moment can help it land.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time you move something to tomorrow, decide the exact time you'll do it.

options.label: I forgot until right now

insight.reveal: Your answer points to promises you make to yourself silently, with no reminder attached. People like this often keep their word to others well, because those promises get written down, while promises to yourself live only in your head and slip. You are likely to be generous with your time elsewhere.
insight.step: Write one promise to yourself in the same place you write promises to others.

options.label: I skipped it, but I kept every promise to others

insight.reveal: This answer suggests you are deeply reliable for everyone except yourself. People like this tend to be the colleague who covers the extra shift and the friend who answers late at night, while their own needs drift to the bottom of the list without a sound.
insight.step: This week, treat one promise to yourself like a meeting with someone you respect.

followUp.prompt: Did you make yourself a small promise today? What happened to it?

options.label: I kept it
options.reflection: Keeping a promise to yourself builds a quiet kind of trust that grows over time. It may feel small, but it often matters more than it seems. Tomorrow, you could make another small one and let yourself enjoy keeping it.

options.label: I moved it to tomorrow
options.reflection: Moving a promise to tomorrow is very human, especially when today was full. The risk is that tomorrow keeps moving too. You might make tomorrow's version smaller, so it's easy to keep before lunch.

options.label: Others' needs came first and it slipped
options.reflection: It sounds like you kept your word to everyone except yourself today. That generosity is real, though your own promises deserve a place too. Tomorrow, you could treat your small promise like a date with someone you care about.

options.label: I didn't make one today
options.reflection: Not every day needs a promise to yourself, and some days are better taken as they come. You may have simply been getting on with things. Tomorrow, if something small feels worth doing, you could quietly commit to it.

questions.prompt: What usually tells you it's time to go to sleep?

options.label: The clock: it's my usual time

insight.reveal: Your response indicates you like days with a clear shape. People who go to bed by the clock tend to keep steady routines with meals and work, wake up with fewer groggy mornings, and can feel a little lost on holidays when the shape of the day disappears.
insight.step: On your next free night, keep your usual bedtime and notice how the next morning feels.

options.label: My body: I just feel tired

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you listen closely to your body's signals. People like this tend to notice hunger, stress and tiredness early, before they turn into a bad mood, and are often good at knowing when to leave a party or step away from work for a break.
insight.step: Tonight, notice the very first sign of tiredness, like slow blinking, and go then.

options.label: The show or video finally ends

insight.reveal: Your answer points to the screen, rather than you, deciding when the day ends. People who sleep this way often say they 'lose' the last hour of the evening without remembering what filled it, yet they also tend to be great at unwinding and know every show worth recommending.
insight.step: Tonight, choose your stopping point before you press play.

options.label: Nothing, I stop when I can't stay awake

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a strong attachment to night as the time that feels truly yours. People like this tend to be creative and alert late in the evening, and going to bed can feel like handing the day back to everyone else, so they often hold on until their eyes close on their own.
insight.step: Tomorrow, find 20 minutes of 'my time' earlier in the day, then see if bedtime is easier.

followUp.prompt: Thinking of last night, what finally sent you to bed?

options.label: My usual bedtime
options.reflection: Going to bed at your usual time gives your body something steady to lean on. It often shows up as a calmer, clearer next day. Tonight, you might notice how your body feels as that familiar time comes around.

options.label: I just felt tired, so I went
options.reflection: Listening to your body's tiredness is a simple kind of self-respect. It tends to work well when evenings are calm. Tonight, you could notice what your very first sleepy signal is, and try to follow it.

options.label: One more episode or video kept me up

questions.prompt: Your work gets praised in front of others. You…

options.label: Say thank you and enjoy it

insight.reveal: Your choice reveals an easy comfort with being seen. People who accept praise simply tend to make others feel good about giving it, are often generous with compliments themselves, and are likely to remember a kind word for weeks without needing to hear it repeated.
insight.step: This week, praise one specific thing a colleague did, in front of others.

options.label: Pass the credit to the team

insight.step: Next time you're praised, say only 'Thank you, I worked hard on it.' Nothing else.

options.label: Enjoy it, then wonder if they meant it

followUp.prompt: Did anyone praise or thank you today? What did you do with it?

options.reflection: Letting praise land, without pushing it away, is harder than it sounds. It suggests you're able to receive as well as give. Tomorrow, you might remember that moment if a tougher piece of feedback arrives.

options.label: I passed it to the people who helped
options.reflection: Sharing credit often shows you see work as something done together. That's a generous instinct. Tomorrow, you might also let yourself keep a small piece of the praise, since you were part of it too.

options.reflection: Brushing off praise can be a habit learned long ago, often to stay modest or safe. It may mean kind words slide past before you can use them. Tomorrow, if someone thanks you, you could just say thank you and stop there.

options.label: No praise came my way today
options.reflection: Quiet days without thanks are common, and they don't mean your effort went unseen. You might give yourself the recognition today didn't. Tomorrow, you could notice one thing you did well, even if nobody said it.

questions.prompt: You find a mistake of yours that nobody has noticed. You…

options.label: Fix it and tell the people affected

followUp.prompt: Did you catch a mistake of your own today? What did you do about it?

options.reflection: Owning a mistake out loud takes a steady kind of courage. You may find people trust you more for it, not less. Tomorrow, you could be just as fair to yourself as you were honest with them.

options.reflection: Fixing things quietly suggests you care about the work being right more than about being seen. That is often enough. Tomorrow, you might check whether anyone else was touched by it and would want to know.

options.label: No mistakes I noticed today

questions.prompt: A big task is due in a week. When do you really start?

options.label: Mid-week, with a plan

insight.step: Next task, decide in advance how many drafts you'll allow yourself. Then stop at that number.

followUp.prompt: Did you move a bigger task forward today, or did it wait?

options.label: No big task on my plate today
options.reflection: A day without a big task looming is a chance to rest your planning mind. You may notice more room for small, pleasant things. Tomorrow, you could enjoy that space without feeling you need to fill it.

questions.prompt: In a meeting, you have an idea. You…

options.label: Wait for the right moment

options.label: Tell one person after the meeting

options.label: Stay quiet, then hear someone else say it

followUp.prompt: Did you have an idea in a meeting or group chat today? Did you share it?

options.label: I held back and someone else said it

options.label: No moments like that today

questions.prompt: Where do you want to be at work in five years?

options.label: I have a clear target

followUp.prompt: Did anything today nudge you toward the future you want at work?

insight.step: Next group meal, try paying only for your share and see if anyone even notices.

followUp.prompt: Did you share a bill, a cost or a chore with others today? How did it feel?

options.label: We split it and it felt fine

options.label: I paid exactly my share
options.reflection: Paying exactly your share tends to come from a sense of fairness that keeps things clear between people. It's not stingy, it's tidy. Tomorrow, you might notice whether others welcome that clarity too; it often makes things easier for everyone.

options.label: I went along, but it felt unfair
options.reflection: Going along while feeling it wasn't fair can leave a small weight behind, and your sense of fairness is valid. Tomorrow, you might have one easy line ready, like 'shall we each pay for what we had?', so it's there when you need it.

options.label: Nothing to split today
options.reflection: No bills or chores to split today means no small tests of fairness to weigh up. Tomorrow, you might notice the times when someone else quietly covers a bit extra for you, and find a way to thank them.

questions.prompt: When is it hardest for you to tell the truth?

options.label: In small talk, like 'How was your day?'

options.label: When it would hurt someone I love

options.label: When it makes me look bad

insight.step: This week, admit one small thing that makes you look a little less perfect, and watch the reaction.

options.label: When I'm being honest with myself

insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.

followUp.prompt: Was there a moment today when telling the truth felt hard?

options.label: Saying 'I'm fine' when I wasn't

options.label: To spare someone's feelings

options.label: The truth came easily today
options.reflection: A day where the truth came easily can be a sign you're among people you feel safe with. That's worth noticing. Tomorrow, you might spot who makes honesty feel easy for you, and spend a little more time with them.

questions.prompt: You realise you were wrong in an argument you 'won'. What do you do?

options.label: Go back and say I was wrong

insight.step: Next time you hunt for new reasons, ask: 'If they had said this, would I accept it?'

followUp.prompt: Did you notice today that you'd got something wrong? Did you own it?

options.label: I said so openly
options.reflection: Saying you were wrong out loud takes a kind of strength people tend to respect, even if it felt awkward. It shows you care more about the truth than about winning. Tomorrow, you might notice whether it made the other person more open with you too.

options.label: I let it pass without a word
options.reflection: Letting it pass quietly can be fine for small things, and you may still have learned from it. If it mattered to someone else, it might be worth a word. Tomorrow, you might check whether anyone would appreciate hearing 'you were right'.

options.label: I looked for reasons I was right
options.reflection: Hunting for reasons you were still right is a very human reflex, because being wrong can sting. Noticing that pull is the first step. Tomorrow, you might try the words 'I see it differently now' and notice how much lighter they feel.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: A day without being caught out can feel easy. Still, being wrong now and then is part of learning. Tomorrow, you might stay curious about one view that's different from yours, and see what it teaches you.

questions.prompt: When you post about your life online, how true is the picture?

options.label: I rarely post at all

options.label: True, but only the best bits

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you edit your life, like most people do. The interesting part: we tend to compare our behind-the-scenes with everyone else's highlights, and forget we're doing the same editing. People like you often have a good eye for what makes a moment worth sharing.
insight.step: Next time you compare yourself to a post, remember one thing you chose not to post.

options.label: I share the hard parts too

options.label: A bit better than real life, honestly

followUp.prompt: Did you post or share anything about your life today? What did it show?

options.label: The good parts of my day

options.label: The real mix, ups and downs

options.label: I didn't share anything today
options.reflection: A day without posting can leave more room to simply live it. You might notice whether that felt freeing or a little quiet. Tomorrow, you could tell one person directly about something that happened, instead of sharing it widely.

options.label: Follow it, but ask to change it

options.label: Depends on my mood that day

options.label: Skip it quietly

options.label: It didn't come up today

options.reflection: A day without reading or watching anything may mean your time went to other things, or you simply needed a break. Tomorrow, you might set aside a short window for a story you enjoy, if that sounds good to you.

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a belief that a 'no' is just information, not a judgement. People like you tend to negotiate salaries and ask for what they need, and that ease can surprise others, who may need a little more warm-up than you do.
insight.step: Next time you ask for something, add one sentence about why it matters to you.

options.label: Drop hints and hope

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you want people to notice your wishes without you naming them, as proof they care. People with this orientation tend to be highly attentive to others' needs, but others rarely read hints as well as hinters hope, so the test is often failed unfairly.
insight.step: Turn one hint into a plain request this week: 'I'd love it if…'

options.label: Wait until someone offers

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a strong dislike of taking more than your share. People like you tend to be considerate guests and fair colleagues, though the cost can be quiet: good things often go to people who simply asked first.
insight.step: Ask for one small thing this week that you would normally wait to be offered.

options.label: Tell myself I didn't want it anyway

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a sense that, for you, not wanting feels safer than wanting and not getting. People with this orientation tend to seem easygoing and remarkably self-sufficient to others, while a private list of shrugged-off wishes quietly grows inside.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment avoidance, a discomfort with closeness, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Catch one 'never mind' this week and say the real wish out loud instead.

followUp.prompt: Did you want something from someone today? What did you do about it?

options.label: I asked for it plainly
options.reflection: Asking plainly for what you want takes confidence, and it often saves everyone some guessing. Tomorrow, you might notice how the other person responded, and whether asking felt easier than you expected.

options.label: I hinted and hoped they'd notice
options.reflection: Hinting and hoping often comes from not wanting to seem demanding, and it can leave you waiting. Your wants deserve room too. Tomorrow, you might try saying one small want directly and gently, and see how it lands.

options.label: I told myself I didn't need it
options.reflection: Telling yourself you didn't need it can feel safer than risking a no. It may also keep you from getting what would truly help. Tomorrow, you might notice one want and let yourself admit it, even just to you.

options.label: Nothing like that today
options.reflection: You didn't need anything from anyone today, or it simply didn't come up. That's fine. Tomorrow, if you do want something, you might notice your first instinct: to ask, to hint or to let it go.

questions.prompt: How do you most often show a partner affection?

options.label: Small touches during the day

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that affection lives in your hands as much as your words. People like you tend to reach for a partner's arm while walking, notice missing touch before anything else, and may feel a day without a hand on the shoulder as colder than a missed call.
insight.step: Next time your partner walks past, give them a light touch for no reason at all.

options.label: Saying it out loud, often

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests words feel like a promise to you, not decoration. People with this orientation tend to leave sweet notes and voice messages that make partners feel openly cherished, and may worry when a partner says it less, even when every other sign is there.
insight.step: This week, notice one way your partner shows love without words, and tell them you saw it.

options.label: I show it, but rarely say it

insight.reveal: Your answer points to love expressed through action: the fixed tap, the warmed-up car, the remembered favourite snack. People like you tend to give more than a partner realises, simply in a language they don't easily read, and may find the words themselves feel oddly heavy.
insight.step: Pair one thing you do for your partner this week with one sentence about why.

options.label: I wait for them to show it first

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how reaching out first can feel to you like a risk of not being met. People with this orientation tend to hold a lot of affection behind a door, waiting for proof it is safe, and once it is, they are often deeply devoted partners.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance, and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Make the first warm move once this week, small and simple, and notice what comes back.

followUp.prompt: Did you show a partner some affection today? How did you show it?

options.reflection: Showing love through small touches tends to make closeness feel natural and everyday. Your partner may feel that warmth more than you realise. Tomorrow, you might notice how they respond when you reach out.

options.label: I said it out loud
options.reflection: Saying your love out loud tends to leave little room for doubt, and that can be deeply reassuring for both of you. Tomorrow, you might add one specific thing you appreciate about them.

options.reflection: Showing love through actions is real love, even when the words stay unspoken. Some partners may still long to hear it, though. Tomorrow, you might try putting one small kind thought into words.

options.reflection: You didn't get much chance to show affection today, and some days are just like that. Tomorrow, you might look for one small moment, like a touch, a message or a word, to let someone know they matter.

options.label: Cooking together at home

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests romance for you lives inside teamwork. People with this orientation tend to feel most drawn to a partner while doing something side by side, like chopping onions or painting a room, rather than sitting face to face over candles.

options.label: A long talk with phones away

insight.reveal: Your answer points to desire that follows closeness, not the other way round. People like you tend to remember what a partner said far longer than what they wore, and being truly listened to may feel more intimate to you than any candlelit setting.

options.reflection: Talking with phones put away gives full attention, which is rarer than it should be. You both may have felt more heard. Tomorrow, you might set aside even ten quiet minutes to do it again.

options.reflection: Life got in the way of time together today, and that happens to everyone. It doesn't mean the closeness is gone. Tomorrow, you might suggest one small moment just for the two of you, even a short walk.

options.label: Sometimes, if we remember

options.label: Rarely. We're deep in routine

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a relationship that feels comfortable more than close right now. Routine is a real sign of trust, and people like you tend to be dependable partners, though small touches are often the first thing to go and the easiest to bring back.

options.label: Mostly my partner
